newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: ANGLO FIRMS ITS GRIP ON ASHANTI.
newsitem.headline: ANGLO FIRMS ITS GRIP ON ASHANTI.

text.p: Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd has firmed its grip on highly-prized Ashanti Goldfields of Ghana by becoming the largest shareholder in Britain's Lonrho Plc, analysts said on Wednesday.
"They've done it. They're in Ashanti. They will effectively control Lonrho which has the 30 percent stake in Ashanti," said an analyst who asked not to be identified.
Holding a direct 25.9 and indirect 2.2 percent stake, Anglo is also hungry for Lonrho's African platinum, coal and sugar assets, ready to pounce when they are unbundled, analysts said.
Lonrho has said it plans to split its businesses into separate mining, hotels and trading firms.
"Anglo definitely likes bits of it (Lonrho). The African assets could prove attractive," said John Clemmow, investment analyst at Fergusson Brothers.
Once unbundled, Lonrho Sugar would likely be snapped up by Anglo associate the Tongaat-Hulett Group, while coal company Duiker Exploration Ltd would also offer value to the group, Clemmow said.

But he added that while attractive, Lonrho's South African platinum interests could pose a problem in terms of European and U.S. anti-trust and monopoly laws. Anglo American Platinum Corp Ltd is already the world's largest platinum producer.

Before stepping down as Lonrho chief executive, Dieter Bock on Tuesday sold his remaining 18.3 percent Lonrho stake to Anglo under an agreement reached in April which gave him the right to sell at 180 pence per share. Anglo initially bought 7.3 percent of Lonrho securing an option on Bock's further 18.3 percent.
Analysts said Lonrho's shares had been traded substantially lower than 180 pence for sometime and that, having failed to persuade Anglo to raise the price, Bock decided to sell.
Lonrho shares were last at 160 pence per share.

"They (Anglo) didn't buy it. Bock put it. As long as the share price was low, Anglo didn't have to do anything. Anglo sees that the break-up value of Lonrho is substantially above 180 pence. It's a bargain," Clemmow said.
In the course of snatching this bargain, Anglo has forged a strong relationship with Ashanti, one of the world's biggest gold mining companies, analysts said.
"Anglo has approached the new relationship by saying that Ashanti is now an associate company and we will work together," one analyst said.
Anglo chairman Julian Ogilvie Thompson on Tuesday said that Anglo's relationship with Ashanti was "good" and he hoped the latest development would "further enhance that relationship".
Just weeks before the purchase of Bock's last shares, Ogilvie Thompson and senior executives journeyed to Ghana and held talks with Ghanaian president Jerry Rawlings.
Analysts said this meeting was to smoothe the way for Tuesday's deal and convince Ashanti chief executive Sam Jonah and the Ghanaian government that ties to Anglo were beneficial.

"The visit to Ghana was probably to prepare everyone involved for the deal. To get everyone on the same side and promise not to step on toes. Anglo wouldn't want a hostile subsidiary or associate," an analyst said.

"There is no doubt that Ashanti will benefit from Anglo and there is no doubt that Anglo will benefit from Ashanti. Together they can do a lot more than either of them on their own," another analyst said.

He added that it was likely black-led Ashanti, gaining easier access to African states, would be entrusted with Anglo's West African exploration programme, while Anglo would provide resources and technical expertise.
